claims.text: TiVNbTa was originally designed as a single-phase refractory high-entropy alloy.
The initial high-purity TiVNbTa material is a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
Adding trace oxygen and nitrogen causes phase segregation during aging at 700 °C.
Impurity-induced segregation locally depletes strengthening solute elements.
Impurity-induced segregation promotes nucleation of brittle precipitates.
Trace interstitial impurities accelerate spinodal decomposition or phase segregation during high-temperature aging.
The resulting brittle precipitates act as crack-initiation sites under mechanical loading.
Impurity-driven segregation and precipitation cause a loss of toughness.
Impurity-driven segregation and precipitation cause premature brittle fracture under demanding mechanical loading.
Impurity-doped samples will have lower tensile ductility than high-purity samples after aging.
Impurity-doped samples will have lower toughness than high-purity samples after aging.
Impurity-doped samples will show more evidence of brittle fracture than high-purity samples.
High-purity TiVNbTa has balanced mechanical properties and toughness in its baseline single-phase state.
A temperature around 700 °C is service-relevant for the proposed demanding engineering applications.
The hypothesis is intended to apply under high-temperature mechanical-loading regimes typical of demanding engineering service.
Other thermal or mechanical aging phenomena may alter the impurity–toughness relationship.
The controlled comparison consists of impurity-doped and high-purity alloy sets aged at 700 °C for multiple durations.
The hypothesis is falsified if the two sample sets have statistically equivalent ductility and toughness and no impurity-induced segregation or brittle precipitates are detected.
